title: Readers in the margins
bodyMd:
Annotations in old books are often mined for evidence of what readers believed. Yet a note beside a sentence may record disagreement, a quotation copied for later use, or a teacher's instruction rather than the annotator's conviction. One scholar examined a student's heavily marked philosophy text and initially read repeated underlining as endorsement. A surviving notebook showed that the same passages had been assigned for criticism in class.

The discovery did not strip the annotations of historical value. It shifted their significance from private belief to a practice of reading shaped by instruction. Marginal marks are traces of activity, but identifying the activity requires context. Their apparent intimacy can tempt historians to treat them as direct access to a reader's mind when they may instead reveal the demands of a classroom, profession or social setting.
